results.description: The FastMix subroutine (Algorithm 1) computes a^{(k+1)} = (1 + ηa) W a^{(k)} - ηa a^{(k-1)} with ηa = 1/(1+√(1-λ2^2(W))).
results.evidence: In dream_repro/mixing.py, the fast_mix function (lines ~40-52) computes: updated = (1.0 + eta) * mixed - eta * previous, where mixed = W @ current. This matches the structural form (1+ηa) W a^(k) - ηa a^(k-1). However, the momentum parameter η is computed in _momentum() as (1-q)/(1+q) where q=sqrt(1-sigma^2) and sigma=λ2(W). This gives η = (1-√(1-λ2²))/(1+√(1-λ2²)), NOT η = 1/(1+√(1-λ2²)) as the rubric states. The two formulas are numerically different.
results.note: The update recurrence structure is implemented correctly, but the ηa formula diverges from the paper's specification. The rubric is only partially satisfied.

results.description: In Algorithm 2, the initial local variables are set to z0 = 1 z̄0, meaning each agent i initializes z0(i) = z̄0.
results.evidence: In dream_repro/algorithms.py, function `_initial_state` (lines 70-74): x is initialized as `np.ones((cfg.agents, trimmed.n_features))` and y as `np.full((cfg.agents, trimmed.n_samples), 1.0/trimmed.n_samples)`. Both are uniform across all agents — every agent i gets the same initial value z0(i) = z̄0 (ones for x, uniform distribution for y). This directly implements the claim that z0 = 1·z̄0, meaning each agent initializes with the shared value z̄0.
results.note: The combined state z=(x,y) is uniformly initialized across all agents: x with all-ones vectors and y with uniform probability vectors. This matches "z0(i) = z̄0 for all i".

results.description: The initial gradient estimators g0(i) are computed as the average of b' stochastic gradients: g0(i) = (1/b') Σ_{ξ∈B_i} ∇F_i(z̄0; ξ), where b' = n for the offline case.
results.evidence: algorithms.py lines 107–113: `local_large = local_n if cfg.large_batch_size <= 0 else ...` sets b' = n for the offline case; `initial_samples = full` (full local partition); `g = _gradients(dataset, partitions, x, y, initial_samples, cfg)` (line 112) calls `local_gradient` over all local samples for each agent. In `objective.py` `gradient_x` (lines 28–47), `sample_scale = float(local_size) / len(indices)` normalizes by the batch size, so when called with all n local samples the result is the average gradient (1/b') Σ ∇F_i(z̄0; ξ). The `_gradients` helper (lines 77–81) stacks these per-agent averages into g[i], matching g0(i) = (1/b') Σ_{ξ∈B_i} ∇F_i(z̄0; ξ) with b' = local_n = n (offline).
results.note: For the online/mini-batch case (large_batch_size > 0), b' = min(large_batch_size, local_n) rather than n, but the offline case (large_batch_size ≤ 0) correctly uses b' = n as claimed.

results.description: The initial gradient tracker s0 is obtained by applying FastMix to g0 with K0 rounds: s0 = FastMix(g0, K0).
results.evidence: dream_repro/algorithms.py line 114: `s = fast_mix(g, matrix, cfg.initial_mix) if name == "DREAM" else consensus(g, matrix)`. Here `g` is the initial gradient array (g0), `cfg.initial_mix` is the K0 parameter (number of mixing rounds), and `fast_mix` is defined in dream_repro/mixing.py line 46 as Algorithm 1 FastMix. This exactly implements s0 = FastMix(g0, K0).
results.note: The variable `cfg.initial_mix` holds K0. The implementation is conditional on `name == "DREAM"`, which is the relevant algorithm path.

results.description: At each iteration t, the algorithm computes z_{t+1/2} = FastMix(zt, K) if ζ_t=1, else FastMix(zt, K').
results.evidence: In dream_repro/algorithms.py, the DREAM algorithm uses a single mixing matrix `matrix` (returned by `ring_matrix`) for all branches. When ζ_t=1 (large_event=True) it calls fast_mix(..., matrix, cfg.large_mix) and when ζ_t=0 it calls fast_mix(..., matrix, cfg.small_mix). Both branches use the same matrix — the only difference is the number of rounds (large_mix vs small_mix). The rubric claims two different matrices K and K' are used depending on ζ_t, but the code uses only one matrix (K) with different round counts, not K'.
results.note: It's possible the paper uses K and K' to denote the same matrix applied different numbers of times (K^large_mix vs K^small_mix), but the rubric specifically says "FastMix(zt, K)" vs "FastMix(zt, K')" implying two distinct matrix arguments, which is not what the code implements.

results.description: The update rules for x and y are: y_{t+1} = Π(z_{t+1/2,y} + η vt) and x_{t+1} = z_{t+1/2,x} - γη ut, identical regardless of ζ_t.
results.evidence: In dream_repro/algorithms.py, the DREAM branch (lines 124–151) computes x_new and y_new with the identical formula in BOTH the large_event branch (lines 128–130) and the small_event branch (lines 136–138): `x_new = fast_mix(x - cfg.lr_x * s[:, :x.shape[1]], matrix, mix_rounds)` and `y_new = project_simplex_rows(fast_mix(y + cfg.lr_y * s[:, x.shape[1]:], matrix, mix_rounds))`. The only thing that differs between the two branches (ζ_t=large vs ζ_t=small) is `mix_rounds` and how `g_new` is computed — the x/y update expressions are the same regardless of ζ_t. This matches the paper's Algorithm 2 lines 13–14 / 16–17 structure: y_{t+1} = Π(z_{t+1/2,y} + η vt) and x_{t+1} = z_{t+1/2,x} - γη ut, where fast_mix implements z_{t+1/2} (gossip), lr_y/lr_x are η/γη, s are the gradient-tracking vectors (vt/ut), and project_simplex_rows is Π.
results.note: The number of mixing rounds differs between ζ_t branches (large_mix vs small_mix), but the algebraic form of the update rule is identical in both — consistent with the paper's claim.

results.description: The projection Π is defined element-wise as Π(y) = [Π(y(1)); ... ; Π(y(m))] where Π(y(i)) = arg min_{y'∈Y} ||y' - y(i)||.
results.evidence: dream_repro/objective.py lines 88-117 implement the projection. `project_simplex` (lines 88-102) computes the Euclidean projection of a single vector onto the probability simplex {y≥0, sum(y)=1} via the classical sort-and-threshold algorithm (arg min_{y'∈Y} ||y'-y||). `project_simplex_rows` (lines 105-117) applies this independently to every row of a 2D matrix (one row per agent), which is precisely Π(y) = [Π(y(1)); ...; Π(y(m))] from Definition 2.4. Used in algorithms.py at lines 130, 138, 155, and 170.
results.note: The set Y is the probability simplex, consistent with the minimax objective (mixing distribution over samples). The element-wise structure is enforced by the row-wise application in project_simplex_rows.

results.description: The recursive gradient update is: gt+1(i) = ∇̃F_i(zt+1(i); ξ) + (1 - c_t)(gt(i) - ∇̃F_i(zt(i); ξ)), where c_t = 1 if ζ_t=1 else 0.
results.evidence: In dream_repro/algorithms.py lines 124-151 (DREAM branch), the gradient update for the recursive (small-event) case at line 144 is: g_new = g + (g_at_new - g_at_old) / max(cfg.q, 1e-12). This divides the correction term by q, producing g + (∇̃F(z_new) - ∇̃F(z_old)) / q, not the formula g_at_new + (1-c_t)*(g - g_at_old) claimed by the rubric (where c_t=0 yields g_new = ∇̃F(z_new) + (g - ∇̃F(z_old))). For the large-event case (c_t=1), the code does a full recompute (line 132-133), which is consistent with c_t=1 yielding g_new = ∇̃F(z_new), but the recursive branch critically diverges. The DM-HSGD branch (line 158) has the structurally matching formula g_at_new + (1-beta)*(g - g_at_old) but that is a different algorithm.
results.note: The DREAM algorithm uses a 1/q scaling on the variance-reduction correction which is absent from the claimed formula. The claimed formula matches DM-HSGD (beta=c_t), not DREAM's Algorithm 2.

results.description: The stochastic gradient ∇̃F_i(zt+1(i); ξ) is computed using a mini-batch of size b if ζ_t=1, else b'.
results.evidence: In dream_repro/algorithms.py lines 124-145, the DREAM algorithm branch implements exactly this logic: `large_event = bool(rngs[0].random() < cfg.probability)` (line 125). When `large_event` is True (ζ_t=1), it uses `local_large` samples (line 131: `_sample(..., local_large)`, where `local_large` corresponds to the large batch size b'). When `large_event` is False (ζ_t=0), it uses `cfg.batch_size` samples (line 141: `_sample(..., cfg.batch_size)`, the small batch b). The two distinct batch sizes are `cfg.batch_size` (default 64, small batch b) and `local_large` (derived from `large_batch_size`, large batch b'). The gradient `g_at_new` is computed via `_gradients(dataset, partitions, x_new, y_new, samples, cfg)` in both branches, implementing ∇̃F_i(z_{t+1}^(i); ξ) with the appropriately-sized mini-batch.
results.note: The rubric labels b as used when ζ_t=1 (large event) and b' otherwise, but whether b or b' is the larger batch depends on paper convention. The code clearly implements two distinct batch sizes conditioned on the large_event flag, matching the algorithmic intent regardless of label convention.

results.description: The gradient tracker update is: st+1 = FastMix(st + gt+1 - gt, K) if ζ_t=1, else FastMix(st + gt+1 - gt, K').
results.evidence: dream_repro/algorithms.py, lines 125–148: `large_event = bool(rngs[0].random() < cfg.probability)` selects between `mix_rounds = cfg.large_mix` (ζ_t=1) and `mix_rounds = cfg.small_mix` (ζ_t=0). Line 148: `s = fast_mix(s + g_new - g, matrix, mix_rounds)` implements exactly st+1 = FastMix(st + g_{t+1} - g_t, K) if ζ_t=1, else FastMix(st + g_{t+1} - g_t, K').
results.note: K corresponds to cfg.large_mix and K' corresponds to cfg.small_mix in config.

results.description: The output xout is uniformly sampled from the set {x0(1), x0(2), ..., x_{T-1}(m)}.
results.evidence: Searched dream_repro/algorithms.py thoroughly. The DREAM algorithm implementation (run_algorithm with name=="DREAM") maintains and updates x iterates but never collects them into a pool for final uniform sampling. The function returns metrics history (scalar values like primal_value, stationarity_norm, etc.) and the final x is simply the last iterate after all steps. No code pattern matching 'xout = rng.choice(all_iterates)' or any uniform sampling over {x0(1),...,x_{T-1}(m)} exists anywhere in the codebase (grep for 'uniform', 'choice', 'xout', 'x_out', 'output.*sample' found no relevant matches).
results.note: Algorithm 2 line 25 in the paper specifies that the final output xout should be uniformly sampled from the set of all iterates collected across all agents and time steps. This is a standard technique for non-convex optimization convergence guarantees. The reproduction does not implement this — it simply uses the final iterate x as the output.

results.description: The stepsize ratio γ is set according to γ = (1/(2κ+1)) · (ηµ)/(1+ηµ), where κ = L/µ.
results.evidence: Searched all Python files (dream_repro/algorithms.py, dream_repro/mixing.py, dream_repro/objective.py, scripts/run_formal.py, tests/test_core.py) and configs (configs/section4.json). The variable `kappa` (value=0.999) is used exclusively as the gossip/mixing matrix diagonal weight in ring_matrix(), not as the condition number κ=L/µ. No formula involving γ, L, µ, or η appears anywhere. Learning rates are hardcoded: lr_x=0.1, lr_y=1.0. No computation of γ=(1/(2κ+1))·(ηµ)/(1+ηµ) is present. Grep for 'gamma', 'eta.*mu', '1/(2', 'L/mu', 'stepsize_ratio', '2*kappa' returned no matches in code files.
results.note: The paper's κ=L/µ (condition number) is a completely different concept from the repo's `kappa` (mixing matrix parameter). The stepsize ratio γ from Lemma 3.1 is not implemented.

results.description: The experiment uses m = 8 agents connected in a ring graph.
results.evidence: configs/section4.json: "agents": 8. scripts/run_formal.py line 108: default --agents=8, and line 102 in dream_repro/algorithms.py calls ring_matrix(cfg.agents, cfg.kappa). dream_repro/mixing.py implements ring_matrix() as a ring topology where each of the 'agents' nodes is connected to neighbors (i-1)%agents and (i+1)%agents. results/formal/robust_logistic_a9a/config.json confirms "agents": 8 in the actual experimental run.
results.note: The ring graph is implemented via ring_matrix() in mixing.py; the number of agents is set to 8 in all configs and scripts. Both conditions (m=8 and ring topology) are satisfied.

results.description: The mixing matrix W is set as the π-lazy random walk matrix on a ring graph with 8 nodes and τ = 0.999, which leads to λ_2(W) = τ + (1 − τ) cos(2π(m − 1)/m).
results.evidence: dream_repro/mixing.py:ring_matrix() builds the π-lazy ring matrix: diagonal=kappa (τ), off-diagonal neighbors=(1-kappa)/2, giving W=τI+(1-τ)P on a ring, whose second eigenvalue is τ+(1-τ)cos(2π(m-1)/m). Default kappa=0.999 (line 9). In dream_repro/algorithms.py line 18 default agents=8, line 29 default kappa=0.999, line 102 calls ring_matrix(cfg.agents, cfg.kappa). configs/section4.json confirms agents=8 and kappa=0.999. All experiment run logs also show agents=8, kappa=0.999.
results.note: The code uses 'kappa' for τ (paper notation) and the ring_matrix construction exactly implements the π-lazy random walk, yielding the claimed λ₂ formula.

results.description: The robust logistic regression model uses local functions f_i(x, y) = (1/n) ∑_{j=1}^n [ l_{ij}(x) + τ (y_j − b_{ij} a_{ij}^⊤ x)^2 ] where l_{ij}(x) = log(1 + exp(b_{ij} a_{ij}^⊤ x)), and y_i ∈ Δ_N = { y ∈ R^N : ∑_{j=1}^N y_j = 1, y_j ≥ 0 }.
results.evidence: In dream_repro/objective.py, the logistic loss is implemented as softplus(-margin) = log(1+exp(-b*a^T*x)) (line 16: `softplus(-margin)`), and there is no τ (y_j − b_{ij}a_{ij}^⊤x)^2 quadratic penalty term anywhere. A grep for 'tau', 'TAU', 'quadratic', '**2', 'penalty', 'sq_pen' across all .py files returns no matches. The gradient_y function (lines 50-67) computes a uniform-simplex offset plus logistic losses, which does not correspond to the rubric's f_i formula. The rubric's specific form with τ-scaled quadratic penalty and l_{ij}(x) = log(1+exp(b_{ij}a_{ij}^⊤x)) (no negation) is not implemented.
results.note: The code implements a related but different robust logistic regression saddle-point formulation (without the τ quadratic penalty term). The simplex constraint y ∈ Δ_N is present via project_simplex, but the local function formula does not match the rubric's specification.

results.description: The total N samples are equally distributed on the m agents, with n = N/m samples per agent.
results.evidence: dream_repro/data.py, function `partition_dataset` (lines 154-173): line 160 computes `used = (n // agents) * agents` (trimming N to be divisible by m), line 171 sets `local_n = used // agents` (i.e., n = N/m), and line 172 assigns each agent exactly `local_n` contiguous samples via `indices = [np.arange(i * local_n, (i + 1) * local_n, ...) for i in range(agents)]`. This function is used by the experiment scripts for the a9a, w8a, and ijcnn1 datasets.
results.note: The implementation drops remainder samples (drop_remainder=True by default) to ensure all m agents get exactly the same number of samples n = N/m.

results.description: The datasets are “a9a”, “w8a” and “ijcnn1” from Chang and Lin (2011).
results.evidence: All three datasets are explicitly implemented: (1) dream_repro/data.py lines 17-25 defines download URLs for "a9a", "w8a", and "ijcnn1" pointing to https://www.csie.ntu.edu.tw/~cjlin/libsvmtools/ (Chang and Lin's LIBSVM repository). (2) scripts/run_formal.py line 105 defines --dataset choices=["a9a","w8a","ijcnn1"] and line 116 runs all three by default. (3) configs/section4.json line 23 lists "datasets": ["a9a","w8a","ijcnn1"]. (4) Results directories results/formal/robust_logistic_a9a/, results/formal/robust_logistic_w8a/, and results/formal/robust_logistic_ijcnn1/ all exist with metrics.csv, run.log, and provenance.json files confirming actual execution on each dataset. Actual dataset files are present in .run-data/.
results.note: The datasets are sourced from the LIBSVM tools website (csie.ntu.edu.tw/~cjlin/libsvmtools), which is the canonical source for Chang and Lin (2011). The repository does not explicitly cite "Chang and Lin (2011)" in code but uses their standard LIBSVM dataset repository URLs.

results.description: All algorithms are implemented by MPI to simulate the distributed training scenario.
results.evidence: dream_repro/algorithms.py implements all five algorithms (DREAM, DM-HSGD, GT-DA, GT-GDA, GT-SRVR) using pure NumPy, simulating multiple agents as array rows (e.g., x shape=(agents, features)). No MPI calls exist anywhere. The only MPI references are comments (line 98: "dataset is trimmed exactly as the MPI reference"). requirements.txt contains only numpy, matplotlib, pytest — no mpi4py. dream_repro/data.py line 155 also only mentions MPI in a comment about partitioning logic, not actual usage.
results.note: The code simulates distributed training by vectorizing over the agent dimension in NumPy arrays, which is functionally equivalent but does NOT use MPI for actual distributed/parallel execution.
